WEEK 1&2: FAMILY HEALTH (DISEASES) OBJECTIVES: At the end of this lesson, students should be able to: 1. Identify the two major types of diseases. 2. Highlight two vectors and the diseases they carry. 3. Analyze the consequences of contracting diseases or infections. 4. Describe ways of disease control and prevention; and 5. What are disease vectors? DISEASE: Can be defined as a deviation of the living organism from the normal state of health, which shows the visible symptoms. i.e., an illness, a sickness, an ailment/ is the disruption of normal body functions, which may alter a person’s normal work and social activities. Disease occurs when the microorganism, which causes the disease, enters the body and overcomes the body defense, causing illness or unhealthy condition of the body. TYPES OF DISEASES When we suffer from one sickness or another, it is said that we have a disease. For example, frequent stooling is usually associated with diarrhoea disease. Generally, if an organism does not have any disease, it is considered to be healthy. Disease can be grouped into two major classes, communicable diseases and non- communicable diseases. COMMUNICABLE (INFECTIOUS) DISEASES:are diseases that can be passed from one organism to another. Such diseases are caused by bacteria, viruses etc. Examples of communicable are measles, chicken pox, tuberculosis (TB), etc. These diseases are usually caused by organisms called pathogens. NON-COMMUNICABLE (NON INFECTIOUS) DISEASES: are diseases which cannot be passed from one organism to another. These diseases are linked with nutrition (e.g. food deficiency) such as kwashiorkor or linked to ageing or environment. Some diseases may also be inherited. Others are cancer, heart disease, ulcer etc. DISEASE VECTORS

Vectors are agents that pass pathogens from one living organism to another. The vector itself is not affected by the disease. Common examples of disease vectors are insects (mosquito, tsetse fly, house fly, black fly etc.), dogs (rabies), and rats (food poisoning Salmonella) DISEASE PREVENTION Some of the ways diseases can be controlled and prevented include proper sanitation, proper health education, knowledge of the life history of the disease-causing micro- organisms, immunization, choice of life partners to control diseases such as sickle cell anaemia and treatment of infected persons. SANITATION It is well known that disease-causing organisms thrive in dirty environments. Disease can be prevented by maintaining a clean environment. This can be done in several ways. First of all, it is necessary to drain all stagnant water to prevent mosquitoes and insects from breeding in them. Oil can also be sprayed on stagnant water. Cleanliness of the home- clothes, utensils, floor, toilets, use of disinfectants, etc. all helps to control and prevent the spread of diseases. Clearing and burning of bushes also help to maintain a clean environment and control the spread of diseases. HEALTH-EDUCATION Some people lack the awareness of the causes of diseases, how they spread and how they can be prevented. Educating people about these will create the awareness and enable such person to take preventive measures against contracting diseases. Education plays a major role in the control of diseases. The knowledge of the life history of mosquitoes is a good example of how education can help us stop spread of disease vectors by eliminating the conditions necessary for its growth and development. IMMUNIZATION Immunization is the introduction of vaccines into the body to help in fighting disease- causing organisms that may enter the body. Such diseases include measles, poliomyelitis, tetanus, yellow fever, whooping cough and tuberculosis etc. Therefore, the essence of immunization is to stimulate the body to produce antibodies, which give immunity to the body against some diseases CHOICE OF LIFE PARTNERS (Pre- marital medical screening)

Choice of life partners is another way to prevent or control the risk of diseases. The major example is the case of sickle cell anaemia. Knowledge of the genotype of different persons helps to prevent persons with genotypes that can result in giving birth to sicklers. Also, in the case of indiscriminate sexual relationships creates high risk of being infected with sexually transmitted diseases including HIV/AIDS. The choice of a life partner should be finally considered, based on the health status of each. Prospective husbands and wives are advised to carry out diseases screening tests such as HIV/AIDS, before agreeing to marry each other, Screening will help to eliminate hereditary and sexual transmitted diseases. TREATMENT Treatment of an already infected person will help to stop further spread of the disease. CONSEQUENCES OF DISEASE CONTRACTION Contraction of disease results in the person being in a state of ill-health or being described as sick. This can have severe consequences on the individual, family and society. When an individual is sick, the person is not able to carry out his normal activities as a student, worker or others. It also requires the spending of money to buy drugs to take care of the sick person. This is closely related to the family who feels and bears the impact of the sick individual in terms of cost and so on. In some cases, the cost of treatment is so much that it cannot be borne by the family which leads to distress and pain in the family. All these have an impact on the society at large. There is loss of production, wages and income. Also revenue is spent to provide health and medical services. These negative impacts can be reduced by taking actions. SUMMARY • Disease: Can be defined as a deviation of the living organism from the normal state of health, which shows the visible symptoms. i.e. an illness, a sickness, an ailment. • Types of disease are communicable and non-communicable disease. • Disease occurs when the microorganism, which causes the disease, enters the body and overcomes the body defence, causing illness or unhealthy condition of the body.

COMMON EXAMPLES OF DISEASE VECTORS ARE INSECTS Disease vector 1. Malaria Female anopheles mosquito-(plasmodium) 2. Sleeping sickness Tsetse fly-(Trypanosome) 3. Cholera House fly(Vibro cholerae) 4. River blindness Black fly-(onchorcerca) 5. Elephantiasis or filariasis Culex mosquito 6. Yellow fever Aedes mosquito(virus) 7. Rabies Dog 8. Food poisoning, lassa fever Rats(Salmonella) WAYS OF PREVENTING DISEASES ARE 1. Sanitation, 2. Health Education, 3. Immunization, 4. Choice Of Life Partner And 5. Treatment Of Infected Persons. CONSEQUENCES OF DISEASE/INFECTION ➢ -The individual spends money, which could have served other needs, on medicines. ➢ -The individual becomes less sufficient and less productive at work, home or school. ➢ -The individual’s contribution to the economy of the family and the society becomes less. ➢ -The family spends money more money on medicines, thereby affecting the family budget. ➢ -The individual spends money, which could have served other needs, on medicines ➢ -The overall productivity of the society is reduced. ➢ -The government will spend more on health of the nation. ➢ -The workforce of the society will be reduced. WEEK 3: REPRODUCTIVE HEALTH OBJECTIVES: At the end of this lesson, students should be able to: 1. Identify the myths about breastfeeding 2. Highlight breastfeeding and its advantages. 3. Outline causes of infant mortality. 4. Explain the meaning of genetic counselling. 5. Define the word reproductive health. REPRODUCTIVE HEALTH Is a state of complete physical, mental, social wellbeing and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity in all matters relating to reproductive system. Reproductive health is the ability to have a satisfying and safe sex life, capability to reproduce and freedom to decide, if, when and how often to do so. Men and women of all ages must care for their reproductive health in order to attain an excellent physical, social and mental wellbeing. GENETIC COUNSELLING It is important for parents to find out about the genes in individual family before getting married. Find out if there characteristic disorders in the families. Genetic counselling should be done in a good hospital, where the pregnant will be told about sex determination of a baby and the effects of genetics on a baby’s eye, hair, skin, colour, height etc. This will help people with family genetic disorder make decision about having children. BREAST FEEDING It is always good to breastfeed babies. Within the first hours after delivery, the mammary gland (breast) begins to secrete milk which is very good for baby. The breast milk contains nutritional elements and antibodies which give the baby temporary immunity to infectious disease. The baby is usually breast fed, but when breast milk is not adequate for the baby’s needs, the baby may be given some other milk forms in addition. Commonly used

artificial milk is cow’s milk prepared in a special way for use by human babies. However, there is no better milk for human babies than human milk in the sense that: 1. It is readily available. 2. It is at normal body temperature. 3. There is no risk of contamination. 4. It helps the uterus/womb back to its normal place soon after delivery. 5. It promotes emotional connection between mother and child. 6. Above all it is very cheap. During breast feeding the nursing mother must be cautious of using alcohol and doctor’s unprescribed drugs. MYTHS ABOUT BREAST-FEEDING The following statements must be dispelled: 1. Once you are breast-feeding, no pregnancy can occur if you have sexual intercourse. It has been found that some women ovulate during breast feeding, so such a woman can get pregnant. 2. You should not have sexual intercourse when you are breast-feeding so that the baby does not suck sperm in the breast milk. (False) 3. Processed milk is better than breast milk. (False) 4. Breast feeding babies need extra vitamin D. 5. A breast-feeding mother should wash her nipples each time before breast-feeding the baby. 6. It is easier to bottle feed than to breast feed. 7. Breast feeding ties the mother down. 8. If the mother has an infection, she should stop breast feeding. 9. If the baby has diarrhoea/vomiting, the mother should stop breast feeding. 10.If the mother is taking medicine, she should not breast feed.

COUNSELLING AND TESTING FOR HIV People living with HIV and AIDS require information, counselling, care and support. In general, they should be advised to: 1. Protect them against any form of sexually transmitted infection. 2. Avoid passing the infection to others through unprotected sexual intercourse. 3. Share information about their HIV status with their spouses and those they trust. 4. Eat nourishing food and take plenty of water. 5. Seek counselling about pregnancy for the health of both the mother and the child. STUDY QUESTIONS 1. What is reproductive health. 2. Mention (5) myths about breastfeeding 3. Highlight (4)importance of breastfeeding 4. What do you understand by infant mortality. 5. Outline (3) causes of infant mortality. 6. Explain the meaning of genetic counselling. 7. Outline three importance of prenatal care. 8. What are the risk factors for birth defects? 9. What is the purpose of counselling people living with HIV 10. Mention (2) preventive measures for HIV.

WEEK 4: ABSTINENCE- (I) OBJECTIVES: At the end of this lesson, students should be able to: 1. Identify all the benefits of abstinence. 2. Analyze different types of abstinence. 3. Highlight the disadvantages of abstinence. 4. Explain the meaning of Abstinence ABSTINENCE: Is also called CONTINENCE; is the practice of refraining oneself from indulging in something, typically alcohol or sex/ is a choice to refrain from sexual activity or drug addict. BENEFITS OF ABTINENCE • Is a great way to avoid the risks that come with sex like pregnancy and sexual transmitted diseases, until you are ready to prevent and/ or handle them? • It is a safe way to comply with religious and moral codes that prohibit/ discourage sexual activity before marriage. •It can also help you focus on things that are important to you, like friends, school, sports activities, having fun, and planning for your future. TYPES OF ABSTINENCE Food, tobacco smoking, alcohol, pleasure, sexual abstinence, religions, organizations. 1. FAST, FASTING: Abstaining from food. 2. DIET, DIETING: The act of restricting your food intake or your intake in particular foods. 3. HUNGER STRIKE: A voluntary fast undertaken as a means of protest. 4. SOBRIETY/ TEMPERANCE: Abstaining from excess. 5. TOETOTALLING (TOETOTALISM): Abstaining from alcohol. 6. SELF CONTROL, SELF DENIAL, AND SELF DISCIPLINE: The act of denying yourself, controlling your impulses.

7. SAWM: The third pillar of Islam is fasting primarily during the month of Ramadan. Muslims abstain from food and drink and gambling and all pleasures from sunrise to sunset during Ramadan. 8. CELIBACY: Is generally recognized as a voluntary choice to remain unmarried/ engage in any form of sexual activity, usually in order to fulfill a religious vow. 9. ABSTENTION: Abstaining from sexual relations as because of religious vows. 10. INHIBITION, SUPPRESSION (PSYCHOLOGY): The conscious exclusion of unacceptable thoughts or desires. DISADVANTAGES OF ABSTINENCE 1. Many abstainers feel like they are the only people not having sex (although this is far from the truth). 2. People may find it difficult to abstain for long periods of time. Women and men often end their abstinence without being prepared to protect themselves against pregnancy or infection. WEEK9&10:VARIATIONAND CLASSIFICATION OBJECTIVES: At the end of this lesson, student should be able to: 1. Identify different types of variation. 2. Highlight different environmental causes of variation. 3. Describe application of variation. 4. Explain the meaning of the word ‘variation. The millions of types of living things can be organized into categories, where we group together organisms with similar features. This is called the classification system. Variation between individuals in a species can be continuous or discontinuous, inherited or environmental. Species A species is a category within the classification system. Living things of the same type belong to the same species. For example, humans are one species and dogs are another species. A tiger Individuals of the same species can reproduce to make more individuals of the same species. Two individuals belonging to different species cannot normally reproduce together. If they do, their offspring is usually infertile and unable to reproduce. For example, animals called ligers are produced when a male lion and a female tiger reproduce. But a liger cannot have offspring. This means that lions and tigers are different species.

What is variation? All people are human. They belong to the same species. Your friends and classmates may have different eye colour and hair colour. Some will be boys and some will be girls. Some will be tall and some will be shorter. The presence of differences between living things of the same species is called variation. Variation between different species is always greater than the variation within a species. Continuous & discontinuous Some of the features of the different organisms in a species show continuous variation, and some features show discontinuous variation. Continuous variation Human height is an example of continuous variation. Height ranges from that of the shortest person in the world to that of the tallest person. Any height is possible between these values. So it is continuous variation. For any species a characteristic that changes gradually over a range of values shows continuous variation. Examples of such characteristics are: • height • weight • foot length. If you record the heights of a group of people and draw a graph of your results, it usually looks something like this:

The more people you measure, and the smaller the categories you use, the closer the results will be to the curved line. This shape of graph is typical of a feature with continuous variation. Weight and foot length would give graphs similar in shape to this. Discontinuous variation Human blood group is an example of discontinuous variation. There are only 4 types of blood group. There are no other possibilities and there are no values in between. So this is discontinuous variation. A characteristic of any species with only a limited number of possible values shows discontinuous variation. Here are some examples: • gender (male or female) • blood group (A, B, AB or O) • eye colour.

Inherited & environmental Some variation within a species is inherited, and some variation is due to the environment. Inherited causes of variation Variation in a characteristic that is a result of genetic inheritance from the parents is called inherited variation. Children usually look a little like their father, and a little like their mother, but they will not be identical to either of their parents. This is because they get half of their inherited features from each parent. Each egg cell and each sperm cell contain half of the genetic information needed for an individual. When these join at fertilization a new cell is formed with all the genetic information needed for an individual. Here are some examples of inherited variation in humans: • eye colour • hair colour • skin colour • lobed or lobe less ears.

Gender is inherited variation too, because whether you are male or female is a result of the genes you inherited from your parents. Environmental causes of variation Characteristics of animal and plant species can be affected by factors such as climate, diet, accidents, culture and lifestyle. For example, if you eat too much you will become heavier, and if you eat too little you will become lighter. A plant in the shade of a big tree will grow taller as it tries to reach more light. Variation caused by the surroundings is called environmental variation. Here are some other examples of features that show environmental variation: • your language and religion

• flower colour in hydrangeas - these plants produce blue flowers in acidic soil and pink flowers in alkaline soil. Both types together Some features vary because of a mixture of inherited causes and environmental causes. For example, identical twins inherit exactly the same features from their parents. But if you take a pair of twins, and twin 'A' is given more to eat than twin 'B', twin 'A' is likely to end up heavier. Variety within a species Natural selection Within a population of animals, plants or any living organisms, there will be inherited variations. Within each species the individuals with the variations best suited to the environment will survive better than the others. More of them will survive to reproduce than the others. When they do, they pass on the genetic information for these variations to their offspring. Species gradually evolve in this way. This process is called natural selection. Over time a population can change so much it may even become a new species, unable to reproduce successfully with individuals of the original species. Artificial selection Artificial selection is when people use selective breeding to produce new varieties of a species. A variety is a type of a particular species that is different in some clear way from other varieties of that species. For example, pedigree dogs come in lots of different varieties, called breeds of dog. They may be different colours and sizes, but they are all still dogs. They are all still the same species. Different varieties of dog have been produced by selective breeding.

Different breeds of dogs SELECTIVE BREEDING OF COWS Suppose you wanted a variety of cow that produced a lot of milk. This is what you could do: • choose or select the cows in your herd that produce the most milk • let only these cows reproduce • select the offspring that produce the most milk • let only these offspring reproduce • keep repeating the process of selection and breeding until you achieve your goal. OTHER EXAMPLES OF SELECTIVE BREEDING The key here is to identify the feature you want, and only breed from the individuals that have that feature. Here are some examples of what selective breeding can produce: • hens that lay big eggs of a particular colour • cattle that produce lots of meat • tomato plants that produce lots of tomatoes • crops that are resistant to certain plant diseases. GENETIC ENGINEERING Variation in living organisms can also be created by genetic engineering, also called genetic modification, or just 'GM'. Using laboratory techniques scientists can alter the genetic code within the DNA of a living organism. They can add genes from a different species to an organism's DNA

For example, GM can be used to alter the DNA in a bacterium so that it produces insulin. This is a human hormone and valuable to people with diabetes. Bacteria reproduce quickly, so a lot of insulin can be made quickly and used to help people suffering from diabetes. Ethical questions Some people are concerned that there may be negative aspects to GM. For example, there are people that believe GM is unethical and should be banned. Other people are concerned that there may be unexpected long-term problems of using GM, producing changes that could not be reversed. Such changes could create new pathogens or "superweeds" by the GM organisms breeding with other species. This could cause the natural balance of living organisms in the environment to be upset. Scientists, society and individuals need to think about the advantages and disadvantages of genetic engineering. CLASSIFYING ORGANISMS There are millions of species on our planet. It would be difficult if we just tried to describe and name each one individually. Although species can be very different from each other, many of them have similar features that allow us to put them into groups. Modern classification system In the eighteenth-century Carl Linnaeus started the modern system of putting species of organism into certain groups and giving them scientific names. Each species is given a name using Latin words, so that the same name can be used all over the world. For example, the scientific name for human beings is 'homo sapiens'. Putting different species into different groups according to their features is called classification. The five kingdoms The first big division of living things in the classification system is to put them into one of five kingdoms. These are based on what an organism's cells are like.
